An anagram is a word or phrase that you get by rearranging all the letters of another word or phrase.

That's the heart of it. You take a word, shuffle its letters around, and if those rearranged letters spell out a real, meaningful word (or phrase), that result is called an anagram of the original.

• "listen" → "silent"

Both words are made of the exact same six letters: l, i, s, t, e, n — just in a different order.

  • "earth" → "heart"

Same five letters: e, a, r, t, h — rearranged to form a completely different word.

  • "cat" → "act"

Same three letters: c, a, t — shuffled into a new word.

Notice that in every case, the two words are made of the same set of letters, used the same number of times — just arranged differently.

For something to qualify as a true anagram, every single letter must be used — no more, no less.

You cannot:

  • Add a new letter that wasn't there originally
  • Leave out any letter from the original
  • Use a letter more times than it appears in the original

For example, "cat" and "car" are not anagrams. Even though they share the letters c and a, "car" has an r where "cat" has a t — they don't share the same full set of letters.

Anagrams aren't limited to single words. Entire phrases can be anagrams of each other, with spaces and punctuation typically ignored when checking:

  • "the eyes" → "they see"

(Letters: t, h, e, e, y, e, s — same in both, spaces don't count)

  • "astronomer" → "moon starer"

(Same ten letters, rearranged into a two-word phrase)

These phrase-level anagrams are especially popular in word puzzles, because a clever one can feel almost poetic — the rearranged version sometimes even relates in meaning to the original, as in "astronomer" and "moon starer."

Randomly scrambling letters doesn't automatically produce an anagram. If you rearrange "cat" and get "tca," that's not an anagram — because tca is not a real word.

An anagram must produce something that actually means something — a real word, name, or recognizable phrase in a language. The magic of a good anagram is that the scramble yields something genuinely useful or meaningful, not just a jumble of letters.
A word can have more than one anagram

Some words are lucky enough to have multiple anagrams. For example, the letters p, o, s, t can be rearranged into:

  • stop
  • spot
  • tops
  • pots
  • opts

All five are anagrams of each other, because they all use the same four letters.

If word A is an anagram of word B, then word B is equally an anagram of word A. There's no "original" and "copy" — the relationship goes both ways.

So "listen" is an anagram of "silent," and "silent" is an anagram of "listen." Neither has a higher claim to being the "real" word.

• Word puzzles and games — Anagram puzzles ask you to unscramble a set of letters into a real word.
  • Crosswords — Cryptic crosswords frequently use anagram clues, often signaled by words like "mixed," "scrambled," "confused," or "rearranged" in the clue.
  • Pen names — Some authors and artists have used anagrams of their real names as pseudonyms.
  • Wordplay and trivia — Pointing out a surprising anagram ("Did you know 'dormitory' is an anagram of 'dirty room'?") is a popular form of wordplay.
An anagram is a word or phrase formed by rearranging all the letters of another word or phrase — every letter used, none added, none dropped — to spell out something new and meaningful.
